sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Build the image (docker build -t myapp .), run the container (docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp). The EXPOSE documents the port; -p maps it. The container runs the CMD's binary with the process isolated.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The commands:

```bash
# Build the image from the Dockerfile
docker build -t myapp .

# Run the container
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 --name myapp-1 myapp
# -d: detached
# -p 8080:8080: host:container port mapping
# --name: the handle for logs/stops

# Verify
docker ps                    # the container is running
curl localhost:8080/health  # the app responds

docker logs myapp-1          # the app's stdout
docker stop myapp-1          # graceful stop
docker rm myapp-1             # remove
```

The binary's relationship to the container: the container IS the process (plus the isolation layers). The Go binary (CMD's target) runs as PID 1 inside the container — the container lives as long as the binary runs. When the process exits, the container exits — the lifecycle is one-to-one.

The port semantics: EXPOSE 8080 in the Dockerfile is DOCUMENTATION (the metadata that says 'this listens on 8080') — it does NOT make the port accessible. The -p 8080:8080 at run time is the actual mapping (the host port → the container port). Without -p, the app is unreachable from outside the container.

The Go-specific signals: a graceful shutdown needs the binary to handle SIGTERM (Go's os/signal) — the container stop sends SIGTERM, waits the grace period, then SIGKILL. Go's signal.NotifyContext integrates with this directly.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B[docker build -t myapp .] → I[image: app binary in alpine]
    I → R[docker run -d -p 8080:8080 myapp]
    R --> C[container: binary as PID 1]
    C --> L[logs: docker logs]
    C --> S[stop: SIGTERM → graceful]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
PID 1 and the signal problem (the Go-specific production detail): the Go binary runs as PID 1 in the container — PID 1 has special signal semantics (the kernel doesn't apply default handlers). Go's runtime handles SIGTERM forwarding correctly, but a naive binary that doesn't handle signals won't receive the TERM — docker stop times out and SIGKILLs (no graceful shutdown). The fix: signal handling in main (signal.NotifyContext) or an init wrapper (tini/dumb-init).

The docker compose pattern (the next step up): one YAML describing the multi-container local environment — the app + the DB + the cache — with networking, env vars, and volumes:

```yaml
version: "3.9"
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://db:5432/app
    depends_on: [db]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
```

docker compose up — the whole stack; compose down — gone. The local-dev environment that mirrors production's topology.
